issues.legal_issue: Goods used solely to cultivate and grow agricultural produce that is later processed for sale are not goods intended for use in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale.
material_facts: The dealer cultivated tea plants and processed the leaves plucked from them in separate factories to produce tea for sale.
The requested fertilisers, chemicals, weed-killers, and pesticides were used for cultivating and growing the tea plants and leaves, not in the factory processing of the leaves.
The cultivation and growth of the plants preceded the manufacturing process, and the court found no direct relationship between the requested goods and that process.
The appeal challenged the refusal to include the goods in the dealer’s registration certificate.
issues.conclusion: The requested cultivation goods were not eligible for inclusion in the registration certificate, and their exclusion was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8(3)(b) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, read with rule 13 of the Central Sales Tax (Registration and Turnover) Rules, 1957, qualifying goods must be intended for use in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale in a specified capacity, such as raw materials or processing materials. J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer holds that the expression can cover processes directly related to actual production, including processes so integrally connected with production that manufacture would be commercially inexpedient without them. Indian Copper Corporation Ltd. v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes holds that intended use cannot be equated with merely facilitating the business. Agricultural cultivation that produces raw material is distinct from the subsequent manufacturing process; rules 24 of the Income-tax Rules, 1922 and 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and Tea Estate India (P) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax were referred to in support of the distinction between agricultural and manufacturing income.

predicates.goods_used_for_agricultural_cultivation: The dealer uses the goods solely to cultivate and grow agricultural produce that will later be processed for sale.
predicates.cultivation_precedes_manufacturing_proce: The cultivation that produces the raw material occurs before the manufacturing process begins.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns refused registration goods used solely in agricultural cultivation that precedes and is not directly related to manufacturing, the cultivation goods are not eligible for registration.

issues.legal_issue: Weighing equipment used in agricultural fields, rather than in the factory manufacturing process, is not eligible as equipment intended for use in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale.
material_facts: The dealer used, or sought to use, weighing equipment in tea fields for cultivation-related purposes.
Weighing equipment used in the factories had been included in the registration certificate, but the requested equipment was for use in the fields.
The appeal challenged the refusal to include the field equipment in the registration certificate.
issues.conclusion: The field weighing equipment was not eligible for inclusion in the registration certificate, and its exclusion was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 8(3)(b) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956, read with rule 13 of the Central Sales Tax (Registration and Turnover) Rules, 1957, equipment must be intended for use in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale. J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. Sales Tax Officer explains that the expression may include goods used in processes directly related to actual production. Indian Copper Corporation Ltd. v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes distinguishes intended use in manufacturing from goods that merely facilitate business operations. Applying the distinction between agricultural operations and manufacturing, the court held that the same reasoning that excluded cultivation goods also excluded weighing equipment used in the fields rather than the factories.
